title: Antibiotics & How Resistance Happens Explained Like You Are 5 (Pharmacology For Sleep & Study)
fullText: Now, before anything else, just let yourself arrive here. You don't have to arrange the pillows perfectly or find the exact right position or make sure the blanket covers both feet evenly. It can be enough just to be lying down or sitting somewhere comfortable, somewhere you don't have to hold yourself upright. Let your shoulders drop a little. Let your jaw soften. Let your hands rest however they fall. There is nothing you need to do for the next little while. There is nothing you need to keep track of and nothing you need to remember when this is over. The words will just keep coming one after another, quiet and steady and you can follow them or you can let them drift past. Either is fine. If you fall asleep somewhere in the middle that is the whole point and if you stay awake that is fine too. There is no test. Before we start, one small thing. This is a calm walk through a subject made for rest and for gentle learning. It isn't professional advice of any kind, medical or otherwise. So, please don't lean on it for anything that matters. And please don't listen to this while you are driving or while you are doing anything that needs your attention. Find somewhere safe, somewhere you can stop moving for a while. If you would like to come back to any of this while you are awake, the nofluff pharmarmacology guide is linked in the description and it covers the same ground in a form you can actually read. But you don't need it tonight. Tonight you can just listen. So let's think very slowly about something small. Something so small that you cannot see it with your eyes alone. A single living thing so tiny that millions of them could fit on the head of a pin and never notice each other. These little living things are called bacteria. And bacteria are everywhere. They are on your skin right now and in your mouth and in your gut. They are in the soil outside and in the water and on the leaves of plants and on the surface of your phone. Most of them are harmless. Many of them are helpful. Some of them, a small number, can cause trouble inside a human body. And for a very long time, people had no idea that these little creatures existed at all because nobody had ever seen one. Now, when a person gets an infection, it often means that some of these tiny bacteria have found their way into a part of the body where they can grow and multiply, and multiply they do. A single bacterium can split into two, and those two can split into four, and those four into eight, and on and on. doubling over and over much faster than you might expect. In the right conditions, some bacteria can double in number every 20 minutes or so. So, a small number in the morning can become an enormous number by the evening and as they grow, they release substances that the body does not like or they damage the tissues they are living in and the person begins to feel unwell. The body fights back of course with an immune system. But sometimes the bacteria grow faster than the body can cope with and that is when a person might need help. That help often comes in the form of a medicine called an antibiotic and that is what these talks are about. Antibiotics and how they work and the slow quiet problem of how bacteria learn to resist them. It is a long story and a strange one and it is full of little details that most people never think about. But tonight you don't have to keep up. You can let the words roll over you like water. And if a thought slips away, that is all right. There is no need to catch it. We will come back around to everything again more than once in different words until it settles. So let's begin at the very beginning. Before antibiotics, before medicines, before anyone knew what a bacterium was, for most of human history, an infection was a frightening thing because there was so little anyone could do. A small cut on a hand could become red and swollen, and the redness could spread, and there was no way to stop it. People tried all sorts of things, of course. They used honey and wine and moldy bread and herbs and prayers. And sometimes these things helped a little and sometimes they did not. But nobody understood why. Nobody knew that there were living things too small to see crawling and growing and multiplying inside a wound. The whole idea would have sounded like magic. Then over time a few careful observers began to notice something strange. There were certain substances, certain molds and fungi that seemed to stop bacteria from growing. In the late 1800s and early 1900s, scientists began to describe these effects more clearly. And then in 1928, a man named Alexander Fleming came back from a holiday to find that a mold had landed on one of his dishes of bacteria. And all around the mold, the bacteria had stopped growing. The mold was producing something that killed them. That something was the first true antibiotic and it was named penicellin. Now the word antibiotic itself is worth sitting with for a moment because it tells you a lot. The word comes from two older words. Anti meaning against and bios meaning life. So an antibiotic is literally something that works against life, but not against all life, not against human life or plant life or even all bacterial life. Different antibiotics work against different kinds of bacteria. And a good antibiotic is one that harms the bacteria far more than it harms the person taking it. The trick is to find something that the bacteria have or do that human cells do not, and then aim the medicine at that difference. It is a little like finding a lock that only the bacteria use and then making a key that breaks that lock while leaving all the human locks alone. That is the idea anyway. The reality is a bit messier because bacteria are living things and living things change. They adapt. And that right there is the whole story in one sentence. Bacteria change and medicines stay the same. And over time the medicines stop working as well. That is resistance and it is not a future problem. It is happening right now all over the world slowly and quietly in hospitals and homes and farms and rivers. But we will come to that for now. Just rest in the idea that bacteria are small, that they can grow fast, and that antibiotics are medicines that slow them down or kill them. Let's take one more small step before we settle for the night. Think about the word bacteria for a moment. It is a plural word. One is a bacterium. Many are bacteria. And a bacterium is not like a human cell. It is much simpler and much older. Bacteria have been on this planet for something like 3 and a half billion years, which is far longer than any animal, far longer than any plant, far longer than anything with a backbone. They have survived ice ages and heat waves and floods and droughts and the slow drift of continents. They have learned to live in boiling springs and frozen lakes and the deepest parts of the ocean. They are in a way the great survivors of the living world. And that matters because when we talk about resistance, we are talking about that ancient ability to survive, waking up and stretching and getting to work. So if you are lying there half asleep and the thought of bacteria feels far away and a little abstract, that is all right. All you need to hold on to is this. There are tiny living things all around us and inside us. Sometimes they cause illness. Antibiotics are medicines that fight them. And the bacteria have their own ways of fighting back. That is the whole shape of the story. It will be filled in slowly, piece by piece, over the next little while. But you do not need to memorize any of it. You do not need to be awake for any of it. You can let your eyes close now and let the next part come to you without reaching for it. A bacterium when you look at it under a very powerful microscope is a little thing shaped like a rod or a sphere or a spiral. It is just one cell. But a cell is not nothing. A cell is a little bag of activity, a little factory with a skin. And inside that skin, there are all the instructions the bacterium needs to live and grow and copy itself. Those instructions are written in a long molecule, a spiraling thread. And that thread is called DNA. Every living thing has DNA. You and me and the grass and the birds and the bacteria. And the DNA is like a recipe book. It says how to build the things the cell needs, how to make energy, how to divide into two. And when a bacterium divides, it copies that recipe book and hands one copy to each of its two daughters. Usually, the copy is exact, but not always. Sometimes, very rarely, there is a small mistake. A single letter in the recipe book gets changed. And most of the time, that change does nothing or it makes things worse. and the bacterium dies or grows more slowly. But every now and then, by pure chance, a change comes along that helps. It might change the shape of a protein just a little so that a certain poison no longer sticks to it. It might build a pump that pushes the poison back out. And when that happens, the bacterium with the helpful change has an advantage. It survives where others die. It grows and divides and passes that helpful change onto its daughters and they pass it on to theirs. And that is evolution happening on a scale so small and so fast that you cannot see it but you can see its effects. And that is the quiet engine behind everything we are going to talk about. Antibiotics kill bacteria but they do not kill all of them and they do not kill them all at exactly the same rate. And the ones that survive for whatever reason become the parents of the next generation. So every time we use an antibiotic, we are in a small way selecting for the bacteria that can resist it. It is not a conscious choice on anyone's part. It is just the way life works. Life when pushed pushes back. But let's not go too far down that road yet. The night is long and there is no hurry. We will come to resistance in its own time and we will come to it gently. For now, just notice how comfortable it is to think about something small and far away. The bacteria under the microscope, the slow churning of DNA, the little errors and the little advantages. None of it needs you. None of it is urgent. It is just happening. The way water moves under ice, the way dust settles on a shelf. And you are here not doing any of it, just listening, just breathing. In a little while, we will start to think about how antibiotics actually work, what they do when they enter a bacterial cell, and what the bacterium does in return. But that can wait. The mind does not need to be full. It can be empty and restful, and that is enough. The words will still be here when you come back. And if you don't come back, that is all right, too. The story is patient. It can wait all night. Let yourself sink a little deeper now. Let the pillow take a little more of your weight. Let the blanket settle around your shoulders. There is nowhere to be and nothing to do. The topic is not going anywhere, and neither are you, and that is exactly as it should be. We are just beginning, but we are beginning in the slowest possible way with no rush and no destination. Just a small creature, too small to see, living its small life and a medicine that learned how to stop it. And the long quiet struggle between the two. That struggle is still going on. It has been going on for longer than any of us have been alive, and it will go on after we are gone. But there is no need to feel anything about that right now. It is just a fact like the fact that the earth turns or that the moon pulls on the sea. Facts can be restful when you do not have to act on them. And you do not have to act on anything tonight. You only have to rest. So rest and let the next words come to you in the dark like rain on a window, soft and far away and without any need of you at all. The first thing to understand about bacteria, the thing that makes them both wonderful and troublesome, is that they are single-sellled. You and I are made of trillions of cells, all working together, each with its own job. A skin cell protects, a muscle cell contracts, a nerve cell carries signals, a liver cell cleans. But a bacterium has only one cell, and that one cell has to do everything. It has to take in food and turn that food into energy. and build the parts it needs and copy its DNA and divide. All of that in a space so small that you could line up a thousand of them across the width of a single hair. It is a marvel really when you think about it slowly. A whole life, a whole inheritance, a whole future packed into a speck. And because a bacterium is so small and because it has no brain and no thoughts, it lives by chemistry. Everything it does is a chemical reaction. It senses its surroundings, not with eyes or ears, but with molecules on its surface that bump into other molecules and change shape. And that change sets off a chain of other changes inside. And the end of that chain is an action. Move toward food. Move away from a poison. Build a wall. Pump something out. It is all chemistry all the way down. And antibiotics are chemistry, too. They are molecules shaped in a particular way that wander into the bacterium and interfere with one of those chains. They are like a wrong key in a lock or a bit of grit in a machine. They do not hunt and they do not think. They just fit or they do not fit. And when they fit, they can stop the whole machine. Penicellin, for example, works by stopping bacteria from building their cell walls. A bacterial cell wall is like a suit of armor on the outside of the cell, holding the insides in and the outside. Without it, the bacterium cannot hold its shape and it bursts. Human cells do not have that kind of wall, which is why penicellin can be given to a person without dissolving the person. It only finds the bacteria or rather it only affects the bacteria because only the bacteria have the machinery it interferes with. That is the lock and key idea and it is the central idea behind most antibiotics. But even as we say that we have to be careful because bacteria are not all the same. A penicellin molecule might fit perfectly into the machinery of one kind of bacterium and not at all into another. Some bacteria have thicker walls or different walls or extra layers that keep the penicellin out. Some have pumps that grab the penicellin and push it back out before it can do anything. And that is not resistance. Not yet. But it is the raw material for resistance. The variety is already there in the population waiting. All it takes is time and the right pressure. And the ones with the pumps and the thick walls and the spare doors become the ones that survive. But we are still in the realm of how things work. Not yet how they fail. So let's stay with the working for a while. Let's think about an infection, a simple one like a sore throat or an ear infection and what happens when a person takes an antibiotic. The medicine goes into the stomach and from the stomach into the blood and the blood carries it everywhere to the throat to the ear to the skin to the gut. The medicine does not know where the infection is. It just goes everywhere diluted in the blood and wherever it meets bacteria, it does its work. The bacteria in the sore throat are stopped and the person begins to feel better. But the medicine also meets the bacteria in the gut, the helpful ones that help with digestion, and it stops some of them too. That is why antibiotics can cause stomach upset. It is not the medicine being cruel. It is just that the medicine cannot aim. It is a little like watering a garden with a fire hose. The water reaches the dry flowers, yes, but it also reaches the delicate seedlings and the path and the cat. the water does not choose. And that is one of the costs of antibiotics and one of the reasons they must be used with a certain amount of care. Not because they are dangerous in themselves, but because they are broad and they touch more than we intend. So now we have a picture soft and slow of what an antibiotic is. It is a molecule shaped by chance and found by human cleverness that interferes with a piece of bacterial machinery. It goes into the body, spreads through the blood, and wherever it finds the right kind of bacteria, it slows them down or kills them. And the body with the bacterial growth stopped can finish the job itself, cleaning up the remains and healing the tissue. The person feels better. The medicine has worked and that is the happy part of the story, the part we all know. But there is another part and it begins the very first time a medicine is used because not every bacterium is exactly the same and not every bacterium is equally affected. A few might have a slightly different version of the target so the medicine does not fit as well. A few might have a way to pump the medicine out. A few might have an enzyme, a little chemical machine that breaks the medicine apart. And when the medicine arrives, the sensitive ones die and the resistant ones survive. And then because the sensitive ones are gone, the resistant ones have more room and more food and less competition and they grow. And the infection, if it comes back, comes back as a resistant infection. This is not something that happens after a long time. It begins on the first dose. But here is the strange part. For a while, nobody noticed. Penicellin was a miracle and it saved so many lives that the small number of resistant bacteria hardly mattered. There was always another antibiotic and then another and another. The golden age of antibiotics. In the middle of the 20th century was a time of great optimism. People thought the problem of infectious disease was solved, that the bacteria were beaten. And in that optimism, antibiotics were used widely, sometimes for things they could not help with at all, like viruses, and sometimes in doses too small or for too short a time. And every use, even the unnecessary ones, gave the bacteria another chance to learn. But that is a later part of the story, and we do not need to go there yet. The night is still young and the body is still settling and the topic is still just a shape in the dark, familiar and not yet urgent. We can stay here with the cell walls and the lock and key idea and the fire hose for as long as we like. The beauty of a long slow talk is that there is no schedule. We can circle back and rephrase and restate until the ideas are as soft and worn as old sheets. And if you are already asleep, then the ideas are doing their work without you and that is good too. So before we drift further, let's say the main thing one more time in the plainest words available. Bacteria are tiny living things made of one cell each and they are everywhere. Sometimes they cause illness by growing where they should not grow. Antibiotics are medicines that kill bacteria or stop them from growing by aiming at parts of the bacterial cell that human cells do not have. And bacteria because they are living things with a long history of surviving can change over time so that the medicine no longer works. That change is called resistance. And the story of antibiotics is the story of that change happening over and over faster than we expected and the quiet effort to understand it and stay one step ahead. That is the whole map. Everything else is detail. The next time you are awake or half awake, we will walk a little further into the detail. We will talk about the different kinds of antibiotics and the different jobs they do and the ways bacteria respond. But that is for another segment, another part of the night. For now, let the map fold itself up and rest on the bedside table. You do not need to look at it again. You do not need to hold the shape of it in your mind. All you need to do is breathe and let the dark settle around you and let the words come to an end for now. The way a wave comes to the end of a beach, slow and soft and without effort. The last thing we were doing before the words ran out was looking at a map. A very simple map with only a few places on it. The tiny living things called bacteria, the medicines called antibiotics, and the slow change called resistance. And if you have been sleeping or drifting or thinking about something else entirely, you have not missed anything. That map is still there folded up. And we are going to open it again now slowly and trace one small part of it with a finger. We ended near the idea of a cell wall. A bacterial cell remember is like a tiny bag and the bag has a skin and just outside the skin there is often a wall, a stiff layer that holds the bag in shape and keeps it from bursting. And penicellin, the first real antibiotic, works by stopping that wall from being built. But that is only one way to harm a bacterium. There are other ways and over the years people have found many of them. So tonight or this part of the night we can walk through a few of those ways one at a time very slowly like turning over smooth stones in a stream. Before we do, let's just restate something very gently because it is the ground everything else stands on. A bacterium is not a miniature human. It is a different kind of thing. altogether. It does some of the same jobs as a human cell, like making energy and copying DNA and building proteins, but it does them with different tools. And that is important because a good antibiotic is one that aims at a tool the bacterium has, but the human does not. If the antibiotic aimed at a tool we share, it would hurt us too, and then it would not be a medicine at all. It would be a poison. So the art of finding antibiotics is really the art of finding differences. And the more we look, the more differences we see. The first difference, the one penicellin exploits, is the cell wall. Human cells do not have a wall at all, just a soft, flexible skin. Bacterial cells, many of them, build a wall around that skin, made of a material that is something like a chainlink fence woven out of sugars and little protein links. The wall is strong, but it is also constantly being taken apart and rebuilt because the bacterium is growing and dividing and the wall has to grow with it. If you interrupt the rebuilding, even for a short time, the wall gets thin and the pressure inside the cell which is quite high makes the cell pop. It is a little like a tire with a weakened wall. The air inside is still pushing out and eventually the weak spot gives way and the tire bursts. Penicellin and its many relatives, the whole family called betalactams, work by jamming the machines that build the wall. They are like a stone thrown into the gears of the wall building machinery. Now bacteria have a second kind of machinery that is also very different from ours and that is the machinery that reads DNA and builds proteins. Proteins are the workers of the cell. They carry things. They build things. They break things down. They sense the outside world. And the instructions for making them are in the DNA. To make a protein, the cell first copies the relevant part of the DNA into a smaller molecule, a sort of messenger. And then the messenger travels to a very complicated machine called a ribosome. And the ribosome reads the message and builds the protein one piece at a time. Bacterial ribosomes are not the same as human ribosomes. They are similar in some ways but different enough that a careful chemist can make a molecule that sticks to the bacterial version and not the human version. That is what many antibiotics do. They jam the bacterial ribosome so the bacterium cannot make the proteins it needs and it stops growing or it dies. These antibiotics have names like tetracycan and ariththramycin and genttoycin and many others. They are not all the same and they do not all stick to the ribosome in exactly the same place. But the idea is the same. Stop the protein factory and the cell cannot live. There is a third kind of difference and that is in the way bacteria make their DNA. Before a bacterium divides, it has to copy its entire DNA. So each daughter cell gets a complete recipe book. The copying is done by a set of tools and one of those tools is called DNA gyraase which is a long name for an enzyme that helps untangle the DNA as it is copied. Human cells have a similar job to do but they do it with slightly different tools and some antibiotics the family called fluuroquinolones aim at the bacterial version of the untangling tool and stop the copying. Without copied DNA, the bacterium cannot divide and the infection cannot grow. It is another example of finding a difference and aiming at it. And then there is a fourth difference, one that is a little less obvious. Bacteria need certain raw materials to grow. And one of those materials is a B vitamin called folate. Human cells get folate from food, but bacteria have to build their own because the bacterial cell wall and membrane do not let folate in easily. So, bacteria have a little chemical workshop for making folate and humans do not because humans simply absorb it. And some antibiotics, the sulfur drugs, stop the bacterial folate workshop from working. They do not kill the bacteria outright, but they stop them from growing. And the body's immune system can then clear the infection more easily. These are called bacteratic antibiotics because they hold the bacteria still rather than killing them. The ones that kill outright are called bacteriaidal. It is a useful distinction and it matters when a person's immune system is weak because a bacterioatic drug needs the immune system to finish the job while a bacteriaidal drug can do more of the work on its own. So now we have a little shelf of different tools. There are wall builders, protein builders, DNA copers, and folate makers. And for each one, there is at least one medicine that gums up the works. But the shelf is not complete, and it never will be because bacteria are not finished finding new ways to live. But we do not need to think about that yet. We are still in the orderly part of the story where the medicine fits and the bacterium stops and the person gets better. And there is comfort in orderliness in the idea that a molecule shaped just so can slide into a pocket on a bacterial enzyme and stop it the way a key turns in a lock. It is neat. It is satisfying. It is the kind of thing you can fall asleep thinking about. Let's think just for a little while about what happens inside the body when one of these medicines is working. Imagine a person with a chest infection caused by a kind of bacterium called streptococcus pneumoni which is a common cause of pneumonia and ear infections and sinus infections. The bacteria are living in the lungs multiplying and the person is coughing and feverish and tired. The doctor prescribes a betalactam antibiotic, something in the penicellin family. The person swallows a pill and the pill dissolves in the stomach and the active molecule passes into the bloodstream. The blood carries it to every part of the body, including the lungs. And there, in the tiny air sacks where the bacteria are growing, the medicine molecules bump into the bacterial cell walls and jam the wall building machinery. The bacteria try to keep growing, but their walls are getting weaker and one by one they burst. The immune system sweeps up the debris. The inflammation settles and over a few days the fever drops and the cough loosens and the person feels well again. That is the story we all hope for and it happens every day all over the world. It is easy to forget in a long slow talk like this one that antibiotics are one of the great achievements of human medicine. They have saved millions of lives. They have made surgery safer and childbirth safer and cancer treatment possible because all of those things depend on being able to control infection. Before antibiotics, a simple cut could be fatal and a burst appendix was a death sentence and an ear infection could spread to the brain. We do not want to think about those things too vividly because this is not the time for fear. But it is worth remembering very quietly that the world we live in is different because of these molecules. The calm we feel when a child's fever breaks is in part the gift of penicellin and its many descendants. And it is not wrong to feel grateful for that, even half asleep, even barely noticing. But the story does not end there. and it never did. Even in the earliest days of penicellin, there were bacteria that did not burst. Some of them had an enzyme, a little chemical pair of scissors that could cut the penicellin molecule apart before it ever reached the wall building machinery. That enzyme is called betalacttoase, and it is one of the first and most important resistance mechanisms ever discovered. It is worth saying the name slowly because it will come back. betalacttoase, a small protein folded into a shape that fits around the penicellin molecule and snips a critical part of it. So the medicine becomes harmless. And the instructions for making that enzyme were written in the DNA of certain bacteria long before humans ever used penicellin. The bacteria that had the instructions could survive and they did and they passed the instructions on. That is a theme we will return to many times. The resistance is not new. It is old. It is ancient. The bacteria have been fighting each other with chemical weapons for billions of years. And the genes for resistance have been circulating in the bacterial world for all that time. What humans did when we started using antibiotics was not invent resistance. We simply turned up the pressure so that the resistant ones which had always been a tiny minority suddenly had a huge advantage and so they flourished. It is a little like pulling weeds but only the ones with red stems. The red stemmed weeds survive and they spread and pretty soon the garden is full of red stemmed weeds and the pulling does not work anymore. But we are not in the garden yet. We are still in the human body, still watching the medicine work, still warm under the blanket. So, let's stay there a little longer and think about the different kinds of antibiotics as if they were different kinds of weather. The betalactams, the penicellin family, are like a heavy rain that soaks the ground and makes the soil too soft to stand in. The cell walls lose their stiffness and the bacteria fall apart. The tetracyclans and macrolytes, the ones that jam the ribosome, are like a long cold spell that slows everything down. The bacteria do not necessarily burst, but they stop growing and the infection stalls. The floricquinolones are like a lightning strike on the copying machinery, sudden and complete. And the sulfur drugs are like a drought cutting off the supply of something essential. So the bacteria starve for folate and cannot multiply. Each kind of weather has its own rhythm, its own pace, its own way of settling over the body. And each one over time has produced its own kind of resistance. The rain produces bacteria that build roofs. The cold produces bacteria that grow thicker coats. The lightning produces bacteria that have lightning rods, channeling the strike away. The drought produces bacteria that find water elsewhere. And the genes for all these adaptations are passed down and shared and swapped until the bacteria in a hospital ward or a farm field or a riverbed are no longer phased by the weather that used to stop them. But that is a later chapter. Right now we are still in the part of the night where the body is heavy and the mind is soft and the details are piling up like snow on a windowsill. There is no need to keep them all. The important thing is only this. Antibiotics work by aiming at things bacteria have that humans do not. And there are several different kinds of those things and therefore several different kinds of antibiotics. the walls, the protein factories, the DNA copers, the vitamin workshops. And because bacteria are living and changeable, some of them have ways to dodge each kind of medicine. But that is not a cause for alarm. It is just the shape of the world, and the world is full of such shapes, and we can look at them without feeling anything much at all. Let yourself sink a little further. Now the pillow is soft and the room is dark and the words are coming in a slow even line like footprints in snow one after another and there is no need to follow them all the way to the end. The story of antibiotics is a long one and we are only just beginning and the beginning is the calmst part. The beginning is where we learn the names of things and the names are not hard and the ideas are not sharp. They are round and smooth like pebbles. And you can hold one in your hand for a while and then let it go. So before we drift any further, let's say the names one more time softly so they can settle in the back of the mind without effort. Penicellin, the first and most famous, the one that breaks the wall. Tetracycl and ariththramy, the ones that slow the protein factory. Fluoroquinolones, the ones that stop the DNA from being copied. Sulfur drugs, the ones that starve the folate workshop, and the enzyme betalacttoase, the pair of scissors that cuts penicellin apart. None of these need to be remembered. They are just words, and the mind can hold them loosely the way a sleeping hand might hold the edge of a blanket. And when the next part comes, we will start to think about how bacteria share their resistance with each other. Not just from parent to child, but sideways from one bacterium to another, even from one species to another, like trading recipes in a busy kitchen. It is a strange and lovely and slightly unsettling idea, and it is the reason resistance spreads so much faster than anyone expected. But that is for later. For now, just breathe and let the words fall away and know that nothing is required of you, not even wakefulness. The bacteria are out there doing their ancient work and the medicines are doing their quiet work and you are here between them resting. And that is exactly right. There is a kind of quiet that comes over a room when the night has been going on for a long time. The noises outside get fewer. The light behind the curtains changes, if it changes at all, and the mind, if it has been listening to a slow voice for a while, starts to loosen its grip on the order of things. One thought drifts into the next, and the next into the next, and there is no sharp edge anywhere. That is a good place to be. That is the place we are in now. And in that place, let's pick up the thread again as gently as we can. We were talking about antibiotics and how they work by aiming at things bacteria have that human cells do not. The cell wall, the protein factory, the DNA copier, the vitamin workshop. And we said in passing that bacteria can share their resistance with each other, not just from parent to child, but sideways like trading recipes. That is what we are going to walk through now slowly because it is one of the most important ideas in the whole story and also one of the strangest to understand how bacteria share things. It helps to remember that bacteria are not like us. We inherit our genes, our recipe books from our parents and we pass them to our children and that is mostly the end of it. A human being cannot in the ordinary course of things pick up a useful gene from a neighbor. If your neighbor has a gene for, let's say, resistance to a certain poison, you cannot get it by shaking hands or by sharing a meal or by standing in the same room. Our genes move vertically from parent to child, generation after generation, like water flowing down a family tree. But bacteria are different. They do not have parents and children in quite the way we do. When a bacterium divides, it splits into two, and the two are, at least at first, nearly identical to the original. That is vertical transfer of a sort. But bacteria can also pick up genes from other bacteria, even from bacteria of a completely different species, even from bacteria that have been dead for a while. They can do this in several ways and each way is a little strange and each way matters enormously for the story of antibiotic resistance. The first way is called transformation and it is the simplest to picture. When a bacterium dies, it breaks open and its DNA spills out into the surroundings. That DNA, remember, is just a long spiraling molecule and it can survive for a time in the soil or water or the fluid of a wound. If another bacterium still alive comes along and bumps into that loose DNA, it can under the right conditions take some of it inside. And if that taken DNA happens to contain a useful gene, like a gene for resistance to penicellin, the living bacterium can stitch it into its own recipe book and begin using it. It is a little like finding a loose page from a recipe book blowing down the street and copying the best recipe into your own book before it blows away. The second way is called transduction and it involves viruses. There are viruses that infect bacteria and they are called bacteriaopages which just means bacteria eaters. A bacteria is an even tinier thing than a bacterium just a little packet of genes in a protein coat and it works by attaching to a bacterium and injecting its genes inside. The bacterium then without meaning to starts building copies of the virus and eventually it bursts and the new viruses go looking for new bacteria to infect. But sometimes during this process a bit of the bacterium's own DNA gets packaged into a virus particle by mistake instead of the viral DNA. And when that virus particle infects a new bacterium, it delivers the old bacterium's DNA along with it or sometimes instead of it. And if that DNA contains a resistance gene, the new bacterium gets a gift it never asked for. It is a little like a delivery truck that was supposed to carry one package, but someone accidentally put a different package in the truck and the truck delivered it anyway. The third way is called conjugation, and it is perhaps the most important because it is deliberate. Some bacteria have a special piece of DNA separate from their main recipe book called a plasmid. A plasmid is a small circular piece of DNA that carries a few extra genes, not the essential ones, but often very useful ones like genes for resistance. And some bacteria with a plasmid can build a thin tube called a pilus that reaches out to a neighboring bacterium and through that tube they send a copy of the plasmid. The receiving bacterium now has the plasmid 2 and the genes on it. This is not an accident. It is a process that has evolved over billions of years and it happens all the time in the soil, in the water, in the human gut, everywhere bacteria live. It is a little like handing a neighbor a photocopy of a page from your recipe book, saying, "Here, this one is useful. You should have it." and the neighbor says thank you and now both of you can make the same dish. So there are three ways and they all matter and they all mean the same thing. Resistance does not have to arise fresh in every single infection. It can spread horizontally through a population of bacteria jumping from one cell to another, even from one species to another faster than any of them can reproduce on their own. A resistance gene that first appears in a harmless soil bacterium can in principle find its way into a disease-causing bacterium in a hospital and then spread through the hospital and then out into the community and then around the world. It is not a quick process, not on human time scales, but it is relentless and it has been happening since long before humans existed. We just did not notice. Now this is a lot to take in and if you are half asleep you may have let some of it go. That is perfectly fine. The names of the three processes transformation, transduction, conjugation are not the point. The point is the sideways movement, the sharing, the way a useful trait can travel through a crowd without anyone's permission. That is the heart of it. Bacteria are not isolated individuals, each with its own private recipe book. They are part of a community, a vast ancient tangled web of genes. And they trade constantly. What one bacterium learns, the whole community can learn. What one bacterium survives, the whole community can become. And that means when we use an antibiotic, we are not just treating an infection. We are in a very real sense teaching a community. The sensitive bacteria die and the resistant ones live and the resistant ones share their recipe and the community as a whole becomes a little less sensitive, a little more prepared the next time that antibiotic comes around. It is not a conscious teaching and it is not a deliberate defiance. It is just the way life works. When life is small and fast and promiscuous, the bacteria are not trying to defeat us. So far we have talked about what bacteria are and what antibiotics are and how the medicines aim at things the bacteria have but human cells do not. We have talked about the ways bacteria share genes with each other sideways and through the community and about the microbiome, the vast crew of helpful bacteria that lives in and on the body. And now the natural next thing is to ask in the most unhurried way how resistance actually comes to be. Not in theory and not in the abstract, but step by step in the real world, in a real infection, in a real person. How does a medicine that works perfectly well today become useless tomorrow or next year or in 20 years? What is the actual sequence of events? The answer, as with so many things in biology, is both simple and endlessly detailed. The simple version is this. Resistance arises by chance and then it is favored by selection. That is all. Chance and selection. A bacterium does not decide to become resistant. It does not sense the medicine coming and muster its defenses. It simply copies its DNA imperfectly. And every now and then, one of those imperfect copies happens to make the bacterium slightly less vulnerable to the medicine. That is the chance part. And then when the medicine arrives, the vulnerable ones die and the less vulnerable one survives and divides and passes on the imperfect copy. That is the selection part. And if this happens enough times in enough places over enough years, the population as a whole becomes resistant. There is no plan and no intention and no escape. It is just the slow grinding of variation and survival. Let's make it even more concrete because concreteness is a comfort. Imagine a single bacterium sitting in a warm dark place in a person's bladder, say, or on a piece of skin. The bacterium is about to divide. It copies its DNA, the long recipe book, and the copying is very good, but not perfect. Out of the millions of letters in the recipe book, one letter is copied wrong. Most of the time, a wrong letter changes nothing because the recipe still makes the same protein or the changed protein is not important. Sometimes the wrong letter makes things worse and the bacterium is weak and it dies or grows slowly and its daughters are outco competed by their stronger neighbors. But every now and then, very rarely, the wrong letter changes something in a useful way. It changes the shape of a protein just slightly so that a certain molecule no longer sticks to it. Or it changes the way a pump works so that the pump moves faster or recognizes a new substance. Or it creates a new binding site, a new pocket that can grab a particular medicine and hold it out of the way. When that happens, the bacterium with the changed letter is not yet resistant. Not in the way we usually mean. It is simply different. It has a variation like a slightly different shade of coloring or a slightly different pace of growth. The variation means nothing until the medicine arrives and then suddenly the variation means everything. The normal bacteria, the ones without the change are stopped by the medicine. They burst or they stop growing or they cannot copy their DNA. The one with the change survives. It is not stronger in any general sense. It is just lucky in this particular situation. The way a person with a raincoat is lucky when the rain starts, but not necessarily better at anything else. And because it survives, it divides and its daughters have the same changed letter and the same raincoat and the same luck. And the next time the medicine arrives, there are more of them. And the ones without raincoats are fewer. And so it goes. This is the basic engine of resistance. And it is running all the time in every population of bacteria everywhere on earth. It is not something that happens only in hospitals or only when people take antibiotics. It is happening in the soil, in the water, in the gut of a cow, in the mouth of a cat. The bacteria are always varying and the environment is always selecting and the result is a slow continuous adjustment of the population to whatever pressures it faces. Antibiotics are just one kind of pressure, but they are a very strong one and they act very quickly. So the adjustment happens quickly too on a time scale we can observe in a human lifetime. But there is a nuance here and it is worth sitting with for a moment because it explains why resistance is not all the same and why some kinds are easier to manage than others. The nuance is this. Resistance can come in degrees. It is not a simple yes or no. Some changes make a bacterium completely indifferent to a medicine so that even a high dose does nothing. Other changes make it only slightly less sensitive so that a high enough dose will still work or a longer course will work or the medicine will work if it is combined with another one. And in the early stages of resistance, the changes are often small. The bacterium is not immune. It is just a little harder to kill. it needs a little more medicine or a little more time. And if the person takes the full course and the dose is high enough, the infection may still clear. But if the dose is too low or the course is too short, the partially resistant bacteria may survive and then the next infection starts from a population that is already partly resistant and the process begins again, moving step by step toward full resistance. This is why doctors so often say to finish the entire course of antibiotics even when you feel better. It is not because the bacteria are counting the pills and will be fooled by a complete set. It is because a short course may kill the most sensitive bacteria but leave the partially resistant ones alive and those are exactly the ones you do not want to leave. finish the course and the idea is that even the partially resistant ones are eventually killed because the medicine is present long enough and at a high enough concentration to get them too. Leave off early and you have done the worst possible thing. You have removed the competition, the sensitive bacteria that were crowding the resistant ones out and you have left behind a population of survivors that are harder to kill. It is a little like weeding a garden and stopping halfway. The weeds that are left are the tough ones, the ones with deep roots, and now they have the whole bed to themselves. The why is that selection is relentless and every interruption is an opportunity and the bacteria do not need to be malicious. They only need to be alive and to divide and to carry whatever variations they happen to have. Now there is another layer to resistance and it is the one we touched on earlier the sideways sharing of genes. Because a bacterium does not have to wait for a lucky mutation in its own DNA. It can receive a whole resistance gene readymade from another bacterium through a plasmid or a virus or a piece of loose DNA and that changes the pace of things. A mutation is a slow step-wise process building resistance bit by bit over many generations. But a transferred gene can confer full resistance in a single moment. One moment a bacterium is sensitive and the next it has a fully functional enzyme that destroys the medicine or a pump that ejects it or a modified target that the medicine cannot bind. This is why resistance can appear so suddenly and why it can spread so fast. It is not that bacteria are mutating rapidly in every infection. It is that the resistance genes are already out there circulating and when a new medicine is introduced, the genes that happen to work against it are suddenly very valuable and they spread. The bacteria in a hospital or a farm or a river already have access to a vast library of resistance genes and the library is always open. When a new antibiotic is invented, it is only a matter of time before a gene is found that can deal with it. The time may be months or years or decades, but the finding is in the long run inevitable. The bacterial world is full of genetic variation and much of that variation is mobile moving from cell to cell and species to species.
