There is tuberculosis which never went away and which has developed strains that are resistant to the standard drugs and require long difficult treatment with secondline drugs. And there is gonorrhea a common sexually transmitted infection which has developed resistance to every drug that has ever been used against it one after another so that the current treatments are the last line and behind them there is nothing or nothing yet. But let's not make a list of horrors. That is not the point of this night. The point is to understand slowly and without alarm how these things happen. And the way they happen is almost always the same. A bacterium with a lucky variation survives a dose of medicine. It divides. Its descendants spread. They acquire more variations, more genes through mutation and transfer. They encounter other medicines. And the ones that survive are the ones with the right combination of defenses. Over time, in the presence of many different antibiotics, a strain emerges that is resistant to many of them. It spreads from patient to patient on hands and equipment and air currents and it settles in hospital wards and nursing homes where the people are more vulnerable and the antibiotic use is more intense. And once it is established, it is very hard to get rid of because the whole environment is now working in its favor. That is the mechanism. It is the same mechanism we have been describing all along, layered and repeated and accelerated. There is no moment of sudden transformation, no single cause. It is the accumulation of small ordinary events. Each one unremarkable on its own. Each one a little like the ones that came before until the weight of them becomes remarkable. It is like the slow silting of a harbor where every tide brings a little more sediment and no one notices from day to day. But after a 100 years the ships cannot get in. The resistance problem is like that. It is built of small things and it is very very patient. Now the response to all of this from doctors and scientists and public health people is not despair. It is careful methodical work. They track resistance patterns so they know which drugs are still working in which places. They design new drugs though the pipeline has slowed. They try to use the old drugs more wisely, saving the strongest ones for when they are truly needed. They improve hygiene so the resistant bacteria are less likely to spread from one person to another. And they try to reduce the use of antibiotics in situations where they do not help like viral infections because every unnecessary use is another round of selection, another inch of silt. None of these measures is dramatic. None of them makes the problem go away. But together they slow it down. and slowing it down is worth doing because time is what we need to find new answers. The body is very still now and the mind may be very far away and that is as it should be. The story of resistance is not a story that needs to be fully grasped in one night. It is a story to be revisited in pieces. The way you might revisit a long novel, reading a chapter here and there, forgetting and remembering until the shape of it becomes familiar. And the shape is this. Living things change. Medicines select, resistance spreads, and the human response is to keep learning, keep measuring, keep caring for the sick, keep trying to stay one step ahead. It is not a battle with a victory. It is a long slow negotiation with the living world and it has no end only a continuing. So if you have stayed awake through all of this you have heard something true and if you have not stayed awake you have still been carried along and either way the truth remains. It is not a truth that demands action. It is a truth that can be held and examined and set down again like a smooth stone in the palm. The stone is not heavy. It is only a fact. And the fact is that bacteria are ancient and adaptable and connected. And our medicines are powerful but finite. And the two are locked in a slow dance that has been going on for less than a century and will go on for as long as there are bacteria and people. And that is not a frightening thought at this hour in this quiet room. It is just the way things are and the way things have always been and the way things will be long after this night is over. Let the words fall away now and let the body rest and let the mind settle into whatever shape it wants to take. There is no more to say right now and nothing more to understand. The bacteria are out there doing their ancient work and the medicines are on the shelf and the people who study them are asleep or awake or somewhere in between and the world is turning slowly in the dark. You do not have to do anything at all. You can just be here breathing and let the rest of the night take care of itself. There is a certain hour in the deep part of the night when the body becomes so quiet that it almost forgets itself. The breathing slows and the limbs grow heavy and the boundary between waking and sleeping becomes thin and unimportant. The words that come to you in that hour do not need to be followed closely. They can come and go like the sound of a distant train or the rustle of wind in a tree outside the window. And if you are in that hour now, then this next part of the story is for you. But it is not for you to hold. It is for you to let wash over you and then let go. We have been talking for a long time now about resistance. How it arises by chance and selection. How it spreads through the sideways sharing of genes. how it accumulates in hospitals and communities and how it turns treatable infections into difficult ones. That is the main thread and we will keep following it. But tonight we can take a small detour because the story of antibiotics is not only a story about medicine. It is also a story about the world and about the ways humans have changed the world and about the unintended consequences of those changes. So, let's think about farms. Not the picturebook farms of story books with a few cows and a red barn and a rooster, but the farms that produce most of the food in the world today. Large farms with many animals kept together in barns and feed lots where the animals live close to each other and grow quickly and are moved to slaughter on a schedule. On these farms, for many decades, antibiotics have been used in large quantities. Not always to treat sick animals, though they are used for that too, but also to prevent disease and to promote growth. The growth promoting use is a strange thing, and it was discovered almost by accident. Farmers noticed that animals given small amounts of certain antibiotics grew faster and put on weight more efficiently. The reason is not entirely clear, and it is still debated, but the effect is real. And so for years, antibiotics were added to feed in doses too low to kill bacteria, but high enough to change the animals gut flora and somehow make it grow better. The problem with this practice, if you have been following the logic of resistance, is not hard to see. Low doses of antibiotics are not enough to kill all the bacteria in the animal. They are enough however to create a steady pressure, a constant selection in which the sensitive bacteria are suppressed and the resistant ones are favored. The gut of a farm animal becomes a kind of factory for resistant bacteria and those bacteria do not stay in the animal. They are shed in the manure and the manure is spread on fields as fertilizer and the bacteria enter the soil and the water and they carry their resistance genes with them and the genes spread through the whole connected web of the microbial world. The farm is not a sealed box. It is part of the landscape and the landscape is part of the planet. Now this is not an argument against farming or against eating meat or against anything in particular. It is just a description of a process. The process is this. When we use antibiotics in large numbers of animals, we create a large reservoir of resistant bacteria. Those bacteria find their way into the environment through manure and runoff and dust and flies. And from the environment, they can find their way to people. Not necessarily directly, not necessarily quickly, but over time the resistance genes from the farm end up in the bacteria that infect humans and the medicines we rely on become less useful. It is a slow, indirect but very real chain of events and it is not only farms. Antibiotics are also used in fish farming in aquaculture where the medicines are sometimes added directly to the water. They are used in plant agriculture, sprayed on fruit trees to prevent bacterial diseases. They are used in dogs and cats and horses and every other animal that humans care for. Each use, however justified, is a little pulse of selection, a little nudge to the microbial world, and the microbial world which is vast and connected and ancient responds. But let's not let this become too heavy. The night is not for heaviness. The fact that antibiotics are used on farms is just a fact. Like the fact that the earth is round or that the moon pulls on the sea. It is part of the world we have made and it has consequences and those consequences are now being studied and addressed. In many countries, the use of antibiotics for growth promotion has been banned because the risk is no longer seen as acceptable. In others, the use is being reduced and alternatives are being sought and the whole question is being re-examined with new eyes. The process is slow and uneven and imperfect but it is moving and that too is part of the story. There is another place where antibiotics meet the wider world and that is in the water. Humans take antibiotics and the medicines do their work in the body but they are not completely used up. A significant part of every dose passes out in urine and feces and from there it enters the sewage system. The sewage is treated but the treatment is not designed to remove antibiotics completely. And so small amounts of the medicines end up in rivers and lakes and coastal waters. And in those waters the same process happens that happens in a person's gut. The low concentrations of antibiotic create a gentle selection pressure on the bacteria in the water and the resistant ones are favored and the resistance genes spread. The river becomes in a very real sense a place where resistance is being quietly manufactured all day and all night without anyone watching. Again, this is not a cause for alarm. It is a cause for curiosity and for careful thought and maybe for a quiet sense of wonder at the scale of the thing. A pill swallowed in a city ends up in trace amounts in a river a 100 miles away and its ghost its molecular presence is enough to nudge the evolution of the smallest living things. The whole planet is connected and the connections are not only in space but in chemistry in the movement of molecules through water and soil and air. The story of an antibiotic is not over when the infection clears. It continues in diluted form through the pipes and the treatment plants and the outfalls into the wide slow water where the bacteria are waiting as they have always been waiting to respond. Now, if you have been following all of this, you may have noticed a pattern. The pattern is that antibiotics once they are released into the world do not simply disappear. They persist in one form or another and they continue to exert their effects. The effects are not always the ones we intended. We intended to treat an infection and we did but we also selected for resistance in the gut and we also contaminated the water and we also created a reservoir of resistance genes in the soil. The medicine is a gift but it is a gift with a shadow and the shadow is long. And yet it would be wrong to end this part of the night on a somber note because the shadow is not the whole story. The shadow is the part of the story that makes the light visible. The fact that we can talk about all of this, that we can map the movement of genes and molecules, that we can measure the concentrations of antibiotics in a river and the resistance patterns in a hospital is itself extraordinary. A 100 years ago, none of this was known. The very existence of bacteria was known, but just barely. And the idea that they could share genes or that a medicine could select for resistance or that the whole planet was a single connected ecosystem at the microbial level was beyond imagining. We have learned so much and we are still learning and the learning is not finished. That is the hopeful part. The ignorance is shrinking. The awareness is growing and awareness in the end is the beginning of everything else. So rest and let the mind settle. The story of antibiotics is not a simple story. It is a story about the body and the world and the slow patient power of evolution. It is a story about human cleverness and human fallibility, about the gifts we have made and the costs we have not yet fully counted. It is a story that is still being written and you are not required to finish it. You are only required to be here in the dark breathing and letting the words come and go. The farms and the rivers and the hospitals are all out there doing their work and the bacteria are doing their work. And you are here resting and that is enough. That is more than enough. The next time the voice comes back, it will pick up the thread again, not with urgency, but with the same slow, even tone. And it will take the story a little further into the places where human beings are trying to solve the problem they have made. But that is for later. For now there is only the quiet and the warmth and the sound of the breath and the slow soft edge of sleep and the knowledge barely felt that the world is large and old and full of small things and that all of it for this moment is at peace. The hours have gathered behind us like a long slow tide, and the body has been still for so long that it feels less like a body and more like a weight, warm and heavy and at rest. If you have been asleep, you have missed nothing that cannot be found again. If you have been awake, you have heard the story unfold in its own unhurried way. And now we are coming to a part of the story that is not so much a new idea as a slow turning of the old one. seen from a different angle. So far we have talked about what antibiotics are and how they work and how bacteria share resistance and how the resistance spreads through the world through hospitals and farms and rivers and the bodies of people and animals. We have talked about the quiet patient power of evolution and about the way a medicine once released never really leaves the world but continues to shape the living things it touches. And now in this part of the night, we can begin to talk about what people are doing in response. Not in a dramatic way, not with a sense of urgency or alarm, but in the same slow, careful, methodical way that all good work is done. Because the problem of antibiotic resistance is not a problem that has gone unnoticed. It has been noticed and it is being worked on. And the work is being done by many different kinds of people in many different places at many different scales. Some of them are scientists in laboratories trying to find new medicines. Some of them are doctors and nurses in hospitals trying to use the old medicines more wisely. Some of them are farmers and veterinarians trying to reduce the use of antibiotics in animals. Some of them are engineers and public health workers trying to keep the resistant bacteria from spreading and all of them in their own way are pushing back against the tide. Let's start with the most obvious kind of work, the search for new drugs. For a long time, this search was very successful. Starting in the 1940s and continuing through the 1950s and60s and 70s, scientists discovered one new antibiotic after another. so many that it seemed the supply would never end. They found them in soil, in molds, in the oceans, in the bodies of insects. They modified them in the laboratory, making them stronger, broader, more resistant to the bacterial enzymes that destroyed them. The golden age of antibiotics was a time of rapid discovery and rapid deployment. And the idea took hold that no matter what the bacteria did, there would always be another drug coming. But the golden age did not last. The easy discoveries were made and the harder ones became less attractive. The new drugs became more expensive to develop and less profitable to sell because antibiotics, unlike medicines for chronic conditions, are taken for only a short time. A drug for blood pressure or cholesterol is taken every day for decades and the company that makes it earns money for decades. An antibiotic is taken for a week or two weeks and then the person stops because the infection is cured. So the incentive to invest in new antibiotics is not as strong as the incentive to invest in other kinds of medicine. And because of this, the pipeline of new antibiotics has slowed and many large pharmaceutical companies have left the field altogether. The result is that we are now in a situation where the bacteria are developing resistance faster than the drugs are being replaced. It is not a crisis of ability. It is a crisis of economics and of attention and of will. But there are still people working on new drugs and they are finding new ways to do it. Some of them are looking in places that have not been well explored, like the deep ocean floor or the microbiomes of unusual animals or the soil of remote caves. Some of them are using new technologies like artificial intelligence and machine learning to screen millions of molecules for antibiotic activity much faster than a human could ever do. Some of them are trying to design drugs that are not antibiotics in the traditional sense but that work alongside antibiotics blocking the resistance mechanisms so the old drugs can work again. These are called adguants or resistance breakers and they are a promising idea. If you cannot make a new antibiotic perhaps you can protect the ones you have. There are also people working on entirely different ways to kill bacteria. One of the most interesting is the idea of using bacteriaophages, the viruses that infect bacteria. Bacteria phasages are very specific and they only attack certain kinds of bacteria, leaving the helpful ones alone. They have been used for a century in some parts of the world, but they have never been fully developed in the west because antibiotics were easier and broader. Now with resistance spreading, the old idea of fagee therapy is being looked at again and in some cases it has been used successfully to treat infections that no antibiotic could touch. The phages are not a cure all and they have their own problems but they are a reminder that the natural world is full of potential medicines and that we have only begun to look. Another line of work is the effort to use the antibiotics we already have more wisely. This is called stewardship and it is a very quiet, very unglamorous kind of work. It involves things like deciding which antibiotic to use for which infection based on the local patterns of resistance. It involves measuring the levels of the drug in the blood to make sure the dose is high enough to kill the bacteria but not so high that it harms the patient. It involves shortening the course of treatment when a shorter course is just as effective because every day of unnecessary treatment is another day of selection pressure. It involves educating doctors and patients about when antibiotics are not needed and why. All of this is slow, painstaking work done by people who never make the news. But it is perhaps the most important work of all because it slows the development of resistance and preserves the drugs we have for as long as possible. And then there is the work of infection prevention. The simplest and most effective way to deal with antibiotic resistance is to prevent infections from happening in the first place. This means clean water and clean hands and clean hospitals and clean surgical instruments. It means vaccines which teach the immune system to fight off certain bacteria before they can cause disease. It means good nutrition and good sanitation and good living conditions so that people do not get sick as often and do not need antibiotics as often. These measures are not glamorous either, but they are powerful and they work and they have been quietly saving lives for more than a century. The point of all this is not to give a report or to reassure or to suggest that the problem is solved. The point is simply to say that the story is not over. The bacteria are adapting and so are we. The race is not a sprint and it has no finish line but it is being run and people are running it and the work continues. There is something deeply calming about that. If you think about it, the world does not simply drift into catastrophe. It responds and adjusts and learns and tries again. The same intelligence that discovered penicellin in a moldy dish in 1928 is still at work, still paying attention, still finding new ways forward. The problem is real, but so is the response. And the response is made of the same slow, patient, cumulative effort that has always been the way of human progress. Let yourself sink a little deeper. Now the night is very old and the body is very heavy and the words are coming more slowly with more space between them. There is no need to follow any of this closely. It is enough to know in the back of the mind that the world is being looked after in its own imperfect way and that the small invisible struggle between bacteria and medicine is not happening in silence. It is happening in full view and it is being met and the meeting is not a battle so much as a long slow negotiation with no end but with no despair either. The bacteria will survive and so will we. And the two of us, the small and the smaller, will keep adapting to each other generation after generation in a dance that has been going on since the beginning of life and will go on until the end. And now perhaps it is time to let the words fall away entirely. The body has heard enough and the mind has heard enough and the night has done its work. The next part of the story when it comes will be just as gentle as this one. And it will pick up the thread without urgency, without demands, without any need for you to be awake. But for now, there is only the dark and the warmth and the slow rhythm of the breath and the knowledge soft and distant that the world is turning and the bacteria are dividing and the medicines are waiting and you are here at rest in the middle of it all. and that is exactly enough. There is a moment in the very late hours when the world outside seems to stop entirely. The traffic is gone and the birds are not yet awake and the house has settled into its foundations and the only sound is the sound of your own breathing and the voice still going, still unhurried, still asking nothing. That is the moment we are in now and it is a good moment and there is no reason to leave it. We have been talking for a long time and the story has grown long and the thread has been picked up and put down and picked up again and now we are near the end of it or near the end of this part of it. And the natural thing to do is to slow down even further and to look back over the shape of what has been said not as a summary but as a way of letting the whole thing settle. The story began with something very small. a bacterium too small to see, living and dividing and carrying its recipe book, its DNA from generation to generation. And we saw that bacteria are not all the same and that their differences matter because some of them can cause illness and some of them can help us and most of them are simply there in the soil and the water and the gut doing their ancient work without any awareness of us at all. Then we saw that humans after thousands of years of helplessness found a way to stop the harmful ones. The discovery of penicellin and the flood of other antibiotics that followed changed the world. It made infections treatable and surgery safer and childirth less dangerous and life longer. It was one of the great achievements of medicine and it still is. And it is worth remembering that even in the middle of a discussion of resistance, the antibiotics are still working every day all over the world, saving lives that would otherwise be lost. But we also saw that the bacteria were not defeated. They were not even surprised. They had been living in a world full of chemical dangers for billions of years, and they had evolved the tools to cope. Some of those tools were the genes for resistance, the little recipes for enzymes that cut antibiotics apart or pumps that push them out or change targets that the medicines cannot bind. And those genes were not new. They were ancient and they were mobile moving from one bacterium to another through the sideways processes of transformation, transduction, and conjugation. The bacterial world is not a collection of isolated individuals. It is a web, a community, a vast tangled network of shared information. And when one bacterium learned to resist a medicine, the whole community could learn it too. And so when humans began using antibiotics in large quantities, in medicine and in agriculture and in the wider environment, the bacteria responded. The sensitive ones died and the resistant ones lived and the resistant ones divided and the resistance spread. It spread through hospitals where the most vulnerable people were gathered together with the strongest medicines. It spread through farms where low doses of antibiotics created a steady pressure toward resistance. It spread through rivers and soil and the bodies of animals until the whole planet was in a sense a single continuous arena for the evolution of resistance. And the result is that some infections are now very hard to treat. The names of the resistant bacteria are not important and they are not meant to frighten but they are part of the story. MSA and the carbopenum resistant gram negative bacteria and the resistant strains of tuberculosis and gonorrhea and the many others that have emerged in the last few decades. They are not new species and they are not more deadly in themselves. They are simply the ones that survived the selection, the ones with the right combination of genes and they are now so common in some places that the old medicines no longer work. But the story did not end there. We saw in the last part of the night that people have not given up. The search for new antibiotics continues in new places and with new tools. The effort to use the old antibiotics more wisely to preserve them for as long as possible is being carried out in hospitals and clinics everywhere. The prevention of infections through clean water and vaccines and good hygiene is quietly reducing the need for antibiotics in the first place. And the whole problem which once seemed so distant and abstract is now being met with the same slow patient cumulative effort that has always been the way of human progress. That is the shape of the story. It is not a story of triumph and it is not a story of despair. It is a story of adjustment of adaptation of the long slow dance between two of the oldest and most successful forms of life on Earth. The bacteria and the humans. The small and the smaller. The one that has been here for 3 and a half billion years and the one that has been here for a few hundred thousand. And the medicines that have been here for less than a century. They are all still here and they are all still changing. And the dance is still going on. And now, as the night deepens and the words begin to thin, the thing to do is not to hold all of this in the mind, but to let it go. The story has been told, and it has been heard or halfheard, and that is enough. The facts do not need to be remembered. The names do not need to be repeated. The only thing that matters is the feeling of having been in the presence of something vast and slow and true. And the knowledge that you are part of it even as you lie here, even as you sleep. So let the breath come and go and let the body sink. And let the mind dissolve into the dark like a drop of ink in a glass of water. There is no more to do. There is no more to understand. The bacteria are out there in their billions and trillions doing what they have always done. And the medicines are on the shelves. And the scientists are in their laboratories. And the doctors are in their wards. And the farmers are in their fields. And the rivers are running to the sea. And you are here in the middle of it all at rest. The last few words are not really content at all. They are just sound and rhythm and the slow fall of a voice into silence. They are the sound of a light being dimmed or a door being closed very softly or a blanket being pulled up over the shoulders. They are a way of saying without saying that the night has done its work and that it is time now to let go and that there is nothing left to hold. So rest. Let the pillow take the weight of your head and let the sheets settle around you. And let the voice fade the way all voices fade in the end into the quiet. The story of antibiotics and resistance will still be there tomorrow and the next day and the day after that and you can come back to it whenever you want and it will welcome you and ask nothing of you and let you go again. And that is all. That is everything. Good night. The night has been long and the voice has been speaking for a long time. And now the words are beginning to run out the way a river runs out into the sea, spreading wide and slow and finally losing itself in something larger. If you have been listening all this time, you have been very patient. And if you have been sleeping, you have done exactly what this was for. Either way, there is no more to learn now and nothing more to keep track of. This is the last part and it is not a summary and it is not a lesson. It is just a slow soft closing the way a book closes when the last page has been read or the way a lamp dims when the night is over. We began a long time ago with a single small thing, a bacterium too small to see, living and dividing in a world that does not notice it. And from that single small thing, we built a picture piece by piece of a whole hidden world. We talked about the cell wall, the stiff outer layer that holds a bacterium together, and about the medicines that break it. We talked about the ribosome, the protein factory that reads the recipe book of DNA and builds the workers of the cell, and about the medicines that jam it. We talked about the DNA copier and the vitamin workshop and the many other small differences between bacterial cells and human cells and about how antibiotics aim at those differences like keys finding locks. Then we talked about how the bacteria answer back. How a single wrong letter in the DNA, a single small mistake in the copying can make a bacterium slightly less vulnerable to a medicine. How the vulnerable ones die and the less vulnerable ones survive. And how survival repeated over and over turns a rare variation into a common one. And how the bacteria do not have to wait for their own mutations because they can share genes sideways through loose DNA and viruses and tiny tubes so that a resistance gene that appears in one place can spread through a whole population and then through a whole world. We talked about the microbiome, the vast community of helpful bacteria that lives in and on the body and about how antibiotics which cannot aim disturb that community even as they fight infection. We talked about sea diff and the quiet danger of clearing the garden and letting the weeds grow back. We talked about the farms and the rivers and the slow spread of antibiotic residues through the environment and about how every use of these medicines, however necessary, adds another small push to the evolution of resistance. And we talked about the resistant bacteria themselves, the ones that have collected many resistance genes and become difficult and sometimes impossible to treat with the drugs that used to work. And then in the last part of the night, we turned a corner and talked about the response. The scientists looking for new drugs in new places with new tools. The doctors and nurses practicing stewardship, using the old drugs more carefully, preserving their power for as long as possible. The public health workers preventing infections so that fewer antibiotics are needed in the first place. The farmers and veterinarians reducing their use of the medicines and finding other ways to keep animals healthy and the slow cumulative effort of all these people working together and separately to hold back the tide of resistance and keep the medicines working for as long as they can. That is the whole story or as much of it as we have told. It is not a story with a clear ending because the process it describes has no ending. The bacteria will keep evolving and the medicines will keep being used and the two will keep shaping each other generation after generation for as long as there are bacteria and people. But that is not a sad thought. It is not even a troubling thought. It is just the way things are and the way they have always been and the way they will always be. Life is change and change is endless and the only thing any of us can do is pay attention and adapt and keep going. And now as the last of the words fall away, there is nothing left to do but rest. The body has been still for so long that it has forgotten what it is like to move and that is good. The mind has been listening or half listening or not listening at all and that is good too. The story has been told and it will still be here tomorrow and the next night and the night after that and you can come back to it whenever you want or you can leave it behind entirely and neither choice is wrong. If you want to remember any of this while you are awake, the no fluff pharmacology guide is in the description and it covers the same ground in a form you can read and study. And if you want to hear the same subject taught properly while you are fully awake and ready to learn, there is a companion channel called No Fluff Academy where the lessons are shorter and sharper and made for the daytime. But you do not need any of that tonight. Tonight you only need to sleep. So let the blanket settle over you and let the pillow take the weight of your head and let the room be dark and quiet around you. The bacteria are out there in the soil and the water and the air and in the warm places of your own body and they are doing their ancient work dividing and sharing and changing without any need for your attention. The medicines are on the shelves and the scientists are in their laboratories and the doctors are in their wards and the rivers are running to the sea. The world is turning slowly under the stars and you are part of it. A small warm presence in the dark breathing in and out and that is enough. The last thing is not a thought at all. It is just a feeling like the feeling of a hand resting lightly on a shoulder or a voice saying very softly that everything is all right and it is all right. The problem of resistance is real and the work to address it is real. But right now in this moment there is nothing that needs to be done. There is no emergency here. There is only the slow fall of night into silence and the slow rise of sleep and the knowledge deep and quiet that you can let go now. Let go. Let the words fade. Let the mind empty. Let the body sink into the mattress, into the warmth, into the dark. The story is over and you are still here and the two things are not in conflict. The story was always just a way of passing the time until sleep came and now sleep is coming and the story has done its work. Good night. And when you wake, if you remember any of this, let it be only the softest part. The part about how small things matter. The part about how life persists. The part about how the world is wide and old and full of quiet wonders. And you are one of them. That is enough. That is more than enough.
fullTextVi: Bây giờ, trước khi làm bất cứ điều gì khác, hãy để bản thân đến đây.
